extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and research-integrity professionals interested in publication quality and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the integrity, quality, and trustworthiness of scholarly articles and editorial processes (detecting fake authorship, fabricated references, data manipulation, inadequate peer review, etc.). Useful for post-publication reviewers, editors, and research-integrity offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship legitimacy (no purchased authorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship must reflect actual contributions; buying authorship (e.g., first-author slots advertised and sold) is misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page reports a dataset (BuyTheBy) documenting ads selling first-author slots for prices ranging from $56 to $5,631. Anti-patterns: advertised/sold authorship, paper-mill facilitated author lists. Detection guidance implied: match advertisements to published titles and investigate suspiciously sudden or purchased authorship positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference existence, accuracy, and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: References cited in a paper must exist, be correctly linked (DOIs/links), and be relevant to the claims they are used to support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page include five cited references that weren’t relevant to their claimed support, nonexistent references, incorrect DOIs/links, and a fabricated reference crediting an author with a non-existent Nature article. Anti-patterns: citations that cannot be located, incorrect DOIs, references that do not substantively support the statement they are cited for, or excessive citations likely produced by LLM hallucinations. Publishers/editors should verify citation existence and relevance before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and image integrity (no manipulation; consistency of source data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures, images and underlying source data must be authentic, unmanipulated, and consistent with the manuscript; image and source-data inconsistencies are grounds for concern or retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents a retraction after finding manipulated data in several figures and errors in image/source-data consistency. Anti-patterns include altered images, mismatched source files, or manipulated figures that change interpretation. Investigation should check raw data, image metadata, and consistency across figures and source files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological transparency and reproducibility (methods, code, and figures must be coherent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods, code, and figures must be appropriate, explained, and sufficient for readers/peers to understand and, where applicable, reproduce the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative problems include flow diagrams whose information doesn’t appear elsewhere in the article, irrelevant MATLAB functions provided with a manuscript, low-resolution data insufficient to support claimed observations, and figures that make no scientific sense (e.g., a sine wave presented as an anatomical structure). Anti-patterns: missing method details, irrelevant or unusable code, figures unsupported by described methods. Guidance: ensure methods and code are directly related to the analyses and that figures are interpretable and supported by data descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review rigor and reviewer expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should be rigorous and conducted by reviewers with appropriate expertise to detect errors, nonsense, or fabricated work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recounts reviewers being baffled by technobabble manuscripts and instances where a reviewer recommended rejection but the paper still advanced; also describes invitations to review the same questionable paper across journals. Anti-patterns: reviewers unfamiliar with the topic, cursory reviews that miss obvious problems, or review processes that allow technobabble to pass. Editors should vet reviewers’ expertise and ensure substantive, critical reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial-board composition and scope alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial-board appointments and reviewer invitations should match the journal’s scope; editors should not recruit out-of-scope researchers for editorial roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Springer Nature launch that invited at least one researcher with irrelevant specialties onto an editorial board for a new agriculture journal. Anti-patterns: editorial boards with members lacking relevant expertise or token appointments that weaken quality control. Guidance: match expertise to journal scope and verify board members’ credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and verification of AI use
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must disclose use of AI tools and journals should require verification of AI-generated content (especially references) to prevent hallucinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A letter claimed to have used AI per journal guidelines yet included fake references, illustrating that disclosure alone is insufficient without verification. Anti-patterns: undisclosed or unverified AI-generated text leading to fabricated claims or citations. Guidance: require explicit AI-use statements and editorial checks for AI hallucinations, particularly validating references and factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and prevention of paper mills and fraudulent services
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and editors should detect and guard against paper-mill products (fabricated manuscripts, paid authorship, fraudulent services) and the marketplaces that sell them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BuyTheBy dataset compiles thousands of advertisements from paper mills; several ads appear to correspond with subsequently published papers with identical titles. Anti-patterns: accepting submissions without provenance checks, ignoring patterns consistent with paper-mill activity. Guidance: monitor social-media and marketplace advertisements, look for suspicious clustering of similar manuscripts/titles, and apply provenance checks and enhanced scrutiny for suspicious submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author identity transparency (use and maintenance of ORCID/profiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should maintain transparent, persistent identifiers and profiles (e.g., ORCID, Google Scholar) to support accountability and traceability of contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes authors’ profiles at Google Scholar, ORCID and other platforms vanishing in cases under scrutiny. Anti-patterns: disappearing profiles, inconsistent identity records, or lack of persistent identifiers. Guidance: encourage ORCID use, require author contribution statements, and check identities during editorial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical reporting and result validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical analyses, sample sizes, and reported significance must be correct and reported transparently; errors that affect significance undermine conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Nature retraction followed editorial findings that some results were “no longer statistically significant,” affecting conclusions, alongside errors in sample numbers. Anti-patterns: incorrect sample counts, misreported p-values, or analyses that don’t match described methods. Guidance: enforce statistical review where needed, request raw data and analysis scripts, and verify that reported statistics support the stated conclusions.
